story.title: The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back

facts.text: Without Huang, the concern among open source community members is that whoever takes over will be more cautious.
Nvidia has named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO.
It’s not clear how Kress will approach the Hugging Face deal or support for the open model ecosystem, but founder-driven priorities tend to get a downgrade when leadership changes.
Huang’s departure also comes as Nvidia has yet to finalize a deal to acquire open source platform Hugging Face for $13 billion .
Still, supporting open source isn’t simply a passion project Huang pursued out of idealism.
It’s increasingly central to Nvidia’s business strategy.
Huang has been a staunch supporter of open source AI, framing the ecosystem as good for safety, innovation, diffusion, and sovereignty.
Huang’s influence extended beyond Nvidia’s investments and product roadmap.
He also emerged as one of the most prominent voices pushing back against Washington’s efforts to restrict the open AI ecosystem.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after he admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, raising concerns about U.S. national security and the motives behind the executive’s support for softer chip export controls on China.

Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads — potential competitors to closed frontier models.
One company insider told TechCrunch that they don’t expect a change in leadership to have an impact on Nemotron development.
Nvidia also agreed to pay $6 billion for a non-exclusive license for open AI coding startup Poolside’s technology.
The question now is whether that commitment can survive without the man who made it a priority.
TechCrunch has reached out to Nvidia for comment.
As some of Nvidia’s biggest customers, including Google and OpenAI, develop their own chips, Nvidia has an incentive to cultivate a much broader ecosystem of AI developers and customers.
Where was Nvidia’s security team? Connie Loizos
Rebecca Bellan is a senior reporter at TechCrunch where she covers the business, policy, and emerging trends shaping artificial intelligence.
Her work has also appeared in Forbes, Bloomberg, The Atlantic, The Daily Beast, and other publications.
Huang also backed companies that would make American open models more competitive, investing in startups like Reflection AI and Thinking Machines Lab.
This article has been updated with information from an Nvidia employee.
“If America fails the man who helped build its future,” the employee in the companywide email stated, “then this world does not deserve Jensen Huang.”
“If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” wrote one anonymous commenter.

An internal “suggestion box” post submitted before Huang’s resignation by a longtime engineer at Nvidia urged the company’s board to take employee sentiment into consideration prior to taking any action.
The submission has attracted more than 1,600 comments since then, with several asking board members to find a way to bring back Huang.

Huang, a 63-year-old who had led Nvidia since its founding in 1993, wrote in an email to employees on Sunday that he had been “unfaithful to [his] wife” and that there was “no excuse.” The acknowledgement followed reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset.
“Nvidia is Nvidia because of Jensen,” the employee tells WIRED.
One employee went as far as sending a companywide email demanding transparency into Huang’s exit.
Over the same period, WIRED couldn’t identify any posts from Nvidia employees in support of his resignation.
They worry the company will eventually suffer without its founder at the helm and say that the board must bring him back.
Are you a current or former Nvidia employee who wants to talk about what’s happening?
Nvidia's board of directors is not considering bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC.
The board is focused on an investigation into Huang, and is not in discussions to bring him back, said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity in order to discuss internal matters.
Nvidia has hired law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead a probe into Huang's conduct and whether it compromised national security or company secrets.
Last week, Huang resigned from Nvidia, the company he founded, after 33 years as CEO.

The resignation came days after Huang admitted to an affair, and news stories alleged he had an affair with Alice Huang, who worked for a customer and is alleged to have contact with Chinese intelligence, as well as affairs with employees at Nvidia.
Over the weekend, the Financial Times reported that Huang had discussed coming back with allies.
Many in the tech world have called for Huang to return as Nvidia CEO.
But here, certain elements make it complicated.
Nvidia's board continues to investigate allegations about Huang's relationship with Alice Huang (not a relative), whom U.S. intelligence says is a spy.

Three House of Representatives committees summoned Jensen Huang for a closed-door interview, and a Senate committee is calling on him to testify to address national security concerns, according to CNN.
Jensen Huang shocked the market last week when he stepped down from his position as chief executive officer at one of the world's most famous companies, Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA).
His move followed allegations of affairs that arose just days earlier.
Though some investors predicted a possible resignation, it still seemed somewhat surprising, as Huang founded the company more than 30 years ago and led its spectacular success story.
Let's consider if a Jensen Huang return really could happen -- and find out what such an event could mean for the stock price.
Today, however, some tech leaders and general Huang supporters aren't ready to say goodbye to Huang.
In fact, they are fighting for him to come back.

A petition for that purpose has drawn more than 176,000 signatures, including more than 92,000 shareholders and several big names in technology, such as Space Exploration Technologies and Tesla chief Elon Musk, and Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke.
The stock could pop initially, but with the potential of new details turning up as investigations proceed, investors might be jittery.
So I wouldn't expect the stock to soar as it did in the past.
The entire market community would be more focused on eventual elements emerging from these investigations and potential legal complications than on the company's path.
So, though the loss of Huang at Nvidia's helm represents a sad and difficult moment, his return might not be the key to boosting the stock.
At this point, the best thing for Nvidia is stability and visibility -- and interim chief Colette Kress may be the best person to provide that right now.

A visionary, Huang always seemed a step ahead and wisely broadened Nvidia's presence across the AI movement through partnerships and acquisitions -- the latest being the decision to buy open-source AI platform Hugging Face.
So, it's not too surprising that many tech leaders wish to bring him back.
And the performance of Nvidia in recent years makes it understandable that shareholders and others also support Huang.

First, a quick note about Nvidia's recent turmoil.

Sporting a leather jacket and speaking about AI in a comfortable, engaging manner, Huang reached superstar status -- and followed through on this by guiding the company along the path of explosive growth.
